newsitem.title: UK: WPP profits gain, promises further growth.
newsitem.headline: WPP profits gain, promises further growth.

text.p: WPP Group Plc, owner of advertising agencies Ogilvy & Mather and J Walter Thompson, posted a 15 percent profit gain in the first half of the year and forecast continuing strong growth.
"The board does anticipate significant further progress even in its reported numbers and even if sterling's strength continues," the company said.

Pre-tax profit for the first half of 1997 rose 15 percent to 78.3 million pounds ($124.2 million). WPP, which generates 80 percent of its earnings overseas, said the profit increase was over 25 percent at constant currency levels.

WPP forecast market growth in five-six percent range in 1998, slightly lower than this year. Chief executive Martin Sorrell said 1999 was expected to produce similar growth but that 2000 may see an improvement.

"In the year 2000 we have the Millennium Olympics, we have the U.S. presidential election, we have the Millennium events as well, which will probably drive expenditure to better levels," Sorrell told Reuters Financial Television.
The first half figures were at the top end of analysts' expectations but WPP shares slipped 3.5p to 270p. Analysts said there had been some profit taking following a strong run ahead of the results.

The company, brought to its knees by the burden of debt in the early 1990s, said average net debt had fallen by 39 percent to 103 million pounds. Debt has been whittled down from 372 million pounds four years ago.
Reported revenue was flat at 830.6 million pounds, the rise in the value of sterling wiping out what would have been an eight percent rise at constant rates.

The company hit its target of a one percentage point improvement in its operating margin, taking it to 11.1 percent. It is aiming to lift its margin to 11.8 percent this year and to 12.8 percent in 1998.
WPP said prospects for the second part of 1997 look similar to the first six months, adding that July revenues appeared to be up almost seven percent if the effects of currencies were discounted.
